scope: Interpretive notes describe named landscape features from the existing source-controlled beach inventory and conditional shoreline-weather principles; no live on-sand or swimming claims.

notes.ludington-state-park: Walk from the shelter of the dunes toward Lake Michigan and notice when the wind reaches you. Hamlin Lake lies behind this landscape, but it is a different body of water. Look at the direction of the waves before deciding what the forecast means for the open beach.
notes.silver-lake-state-park: The Silver Lake dunes lead the eye toward a vast stretch of Lake Michigan. As you move from dune country onto the exposed sand, watch for a change in breeze. An inland thermometer may describe the day well in town without capturing the air you feel beside the water.
notes.holland-state-park: Big Red and the channel entrance tell you that this beach shares the shoreline with a working harbor. Follow the wind across the open sand with your eyes, then check the posted flags. The comfort of a sunny beach day and the safety of the water are separate questions.
notes.grand-haven-state-park: The pier, lighthouse and boardwalk give Grand Haven its familiar outline. Look beyond them toward the open lake: the wind that reaches the sand may not feel like the air along the sheltered streets. Currents around harbor structures demand attention regardless of the apparent temperature.
notes.warren-dunes-state-park: Dunes more than 200 feet high rise behind this Lake Michigan beach. They offer a dramatic backdrop, but the shore itself faces the moving air over the lake. Notice wind direction, the wave pattern and posted flags before you pick a place to spend the afternoon.
notes.muskegon-state-park: Two miles of Lake Michigan shoreline leave room for conditions to feel different from one spot to another. The nearby channel is not the same environment as the open beach. Look at wind direction and the waves; a model forecast is a starting point, not a thermometer at your feet.
notes.pj-hoffmaster-state-park: Behind the long beach, dunes and woods give way to exposed Lake Michigan sand. Pause as you reach the shore and feel whether the wind has strengthened. The sound and shape of the waves offer clues to the lake's mood, while posted notices provide the local safety guidance.
notes.saugatuck-dunes-state-park: Part of this beach's appeal is the walk out from wooded dunes to Lake Michigan. Notice how the air changes when the last shelter falls behind you. Conditions at the waterline may not match the inland forecast, so think about the return walk as well as your time on the sand.
notes.sleeping-bear-dunes-empire: Empire puts village streets close to a remarkable stretch of the Sleeping Bear shore. Step toward the lake and watch clouds move above the open horizon. A warm morning in the village does not guarantee the same comfort where the breeze meets the beach.
notes.sleeping-bear-platte-river: At Platte River Point, fresh river water meets the open reach of Lake Michigan. Watch how the two surfaces move differently near the mouth. Air comfort alone cannot describe currents or swimming conditions where a river meets a Great Lake; look to the official guidance before entering.
notes.frankfort-beach: The pier and lighthouse point toward Frankfort's channel, while a broad beach opens beside it. Compare the breeze in town with the wind over the sand and watch how the waves approach. Keep a respectful distance from hazardous currents near harbor structures.
notes.north-bar-lake: Two waters share this landscape: small North Bar Lake and immense Lake Michigan, divided by a narrow sand bar. Their temperatures and waves need not match. Look at which way the wind crosses the sand before deciding how the day may feel on either side.
notes.petoskey-state-park: Little Traverse Bay opens beyond the beach, where searching for Petoskey stones is part of the visit. A bay does not face every wind in the same way as open Lake Michigan. Notice the direction of the breeze and waves before you judge the water by its clear appearance.
notes.wilderness-state-park: At the northwest tip of the Lower Peninsula, the wide western view gives Lake Michigan the whole horizon. The trees may shelter you inland, but the open shore has fewer windbreaks. Check the forecast and watch the waves before choosing how long to stay.
notes.bay-city-state-park: Saginaw Bay lies shallow beyond the beach, with Tobico Marsh just inland. On a bright day, those two landscapes can have different air and wind conditions. Notice whether the breeze comes across the bay or from land; a distant water reading is not the temperature at the swimming area.
notes.tawas-point-state-park: Tawas Point divides Tawas Bay from more exposed Lake Huron. That makes wind direction a useful clue: two sides of the same point may feel different. Take in the lighthouse view, then look carefully at waves and posted beach information before deciding where to linger.
notes.port-crescent-state-park: Near the tip of Michigan's Thumb, this long Lake Huron beach opens to a broad sky. Wind can be more noticeable on the sand than behind the trees. Watch for changing cloud cover, read the forecast time, and check the actual shoreline before making water plans.
notes.caseville-county-park: Caseville's sand and shallow Saginaw Bay water make this a welcoming shore to explore. Shallow water, though, is not a safety guarantee. Compare the air in town with the breeze along the beach, then check the latest official notices and conditions before entering the lake.
notes.harrisville-state-park: Cedar shade gives Harrisville's beach a sheltered approach. Step out toward Lake Huron and notice whether the wind becomes more apparent. The lake's surface, the posted information and the weather forecast together tell a better story than any single temperature number.
notes.hoeft-state-park: Sand and cobble mark this quieter Lake Huron shoreline between Rogers City and Forty Mile Point. Listen as the water works over the stones and watch the waves' direction. A breeze over open water can feel unlike the air among the trees just behind the shore.
notes.cheboygan-state-park: From the northern Lake Huron beach, Bois Blanc Island is part of the view. Islands, points and protected water can change how wind reaches a shore. Check the wind's direction and the conditions where you stand rather than treating an area forecast as a precise beach reading.
notes.lakeport-state-park: Lake Huron stretches away from Lakeport's open beach north of Port Huron. Clear-looking water does not reveal its temperature or whether swimming is safe. Pay attention to the direction of the wind, then use current park notices and posted guidance for water decisions.
notes.presque-isle-marquette: Rocky points, coves and harbor views give Presque Isle Park several different edges to Lake Superior. A cove can be sheltered while an exposed rock faces the wind. Observe the surface from a safe public place and check access guidance before choosing where to explore.
notes.mclain-state-park: The Keweenaw shore here faces Lake Superior and its long western light. Even on a sunny afternoon, air that has crossed the lake may feel cool against the exposed beach. Check the wind direction and be prepared for the evening to feel different from the inland forecast.
notes.twelvemile-beach: The remote length of Twelvemile Beach makes Lake Superior feel immense. The quiet of the forest behind the sand may not predict the lake's waves. Watch cloud movement and wind before committing to a longer visit, and use the national lakeshore's current access guidance.
notes.sand-point-pictured-rocks: Sand Point occupies a more sheltered setting near Munising than many exposed reaches of Pictured Rocks. Look across the bay and note where the wind is coming from. That geography can change comfort, but the forecast remains a nearby estimate rather than a measurement on the sand.
notes.grand-marais-beach: Grand Marais Bay wraps around a sandy town beach while the open waters of Lake Superior lie beyond. Compare the surface inside the bay with the water toward its mouth. Even here, a calm-looking patch of water cannot replace posted swimming guidance.
notes.whitefish-point: The lighthouse and bird observatory stand beside a far-reaching Lake Superior horizon. Take a moment to watch the waves over the cobble-and-sand shore. Weather and water move independently of the historic sights, so check the forecast and respect the exposed shoreline.
notes.bete-grise: Bete Grise curves into a Keweenaw bay rather than facing the open lake as a straight shore. Its shape may shelter it from some winds and expose it to others. Notice what the waves are doing today instead of assuming a bay will always feel calm.
notes.black-river-harbor: Here the Black River reaches Lake Superior, with waterfalls farther inland. The river mouth and the open lake are distinct moving-water environments. Listen for surf on the shore and check the wind, keeping currents separate from the question of how the air feels.
notes.crisp-point: The lighthouse stands on a remote Lake Superior beach with little built shelter. The wide horizon invites careful watching of clouds and waves, but it cannot tell you exactly when weather will change. Check the latest forecast before the drive and reevaluate conditions on shore.
notes.sterling-state-park: Lake Erie and its coastal wetlands share the landscape at Sterling. The beach may feel breezier than sheltered areas behind it as air moves across the water. Look at the current beach-health and park notices; a comfortable temperature does not certify safe swimming.
notes.luna-pier: Luna Pier's long concrete pier gives this village shoreline a distinctive outline. Watch the waves along Lake Erie, but remember that currents around piers demand special caution. Use the beach-health record and posted guidance separately from the air comfort reading.
notes.glen-arbor-area: Historic Glen Haven sits just behind a Lake Michigan beach in the Sleeping Bear landscape. Walk from the village setting toward open sand and notice whether the wind changes. The air on the shore can feel different from the forecast farther inland.
notes.tunnel-park-holland: The tunnel through the dune gives this beach an unusually vivid weather lesson. Air in the shelter of a dune can feel still, then open Lake Michigan wind greets you on the other side. Read the forecast before you go and the posted flags when you arrive.
notes.pentwater-beach: Pentwater's channel and pier sit beside a walkable harbor-town beach. Look at the waves beyond the harbor and compare the air on the sand with the sheltered streets. Currents around structures require attention even when the weather feels pleasant.
notes.south-haven-north: South Haven's North Beach lies beside the Black River channel and a familiar pier view. Watch the angle of waves arriving from Lake Michigan; it can tell you more about exposure than sunshine alone. Keep channel-current hazards separate from the comfort forecast.
notes.new-buffalo-beach: New Buffalo pairs town streets with a broad southern Lake Michigan beach. A hot afternoon inland can feel different once wind crosses the open sand. Check the issued wind and swim-risk forecast, then read the actual posted flag before getting into the water.
notes.caseville-state-park: Mature pines back Albert E. Sleeper State Park's Saginaw Bay shore. The trees can shelter you from wind that is more noticeable near the water. Compare the breeze in the shade and on the sand, then rely on official park notices for water decisions.
notes.sand-point-saginaw-bay: The Sand Point peninsula reaches into shallow Saginaw Bay, giving wind direction special importance. One reach of shoreline may face more moving air than another. Look at the water where you actually plan to stand rather than borrowing a condition from a distant station.
notes.wenonah-park: Wenonah Park belongs to Bay City's Saginaw Riverfront, not to a designated swimming beach. Enjoy the open views and notice how the breeze differs from sheltered downtown blocks. Nearby lake observations provide weather context, not a measurement of river temperature or currents here.
notes.oval-beach: Saugatuck's Oval Beach is backed by dunes that give way to a broad Lake Michigan horizon. Watch how the grass moves at the dune edge and how the waves reach the sand. A lake breeze can be welcome, but posted beach guidance still matters.
notes.pere-marquette-park: Muskegon's pier and lighthouse sit near a wide, accessible waterfront. The harbor structures offer a landmark, while the open beach catches the full air from Lake Michigan. Compare the breeze with conditions near town and respect currents around the channel.
notes.stearns-park-beach: Stearns Park puts Ludington's town beach, playgrounds and lighthouse views close together. Move from the streets toward the sand and notice the wind. A nearby forecast helps you pack for the day, while actual wave conditions and posted flags shape the waterfront visit.
notes.van-buren-state-park: South of South Haven, dunes rise behind a mile of Lake Michigan shoreline. The woods and dunes may feel quiet while wind moves across the open beach. Read the forecast, then watch what the waves and grass tell you when you reach the sand.
notes.miners-beach: Miners Beach lies under the Pictured Rocks cliffs and forest near the Miners River. Rock, woods and open water each offer a different degree of shelter. Observe the waves from shore and treat the river outlet as a separate current hazard rather than relying on the air temperature.
notes.marquette-south-beach: Marquette's South Beach occupies a more protected reach of Lake Superior than some exposed headlands nearby. Compare the wind around town with the breeze on the sand. A sheltered setting can still have cold water and changing swimming conditions, so check the official guidance.
notes.oscoda-beach-park: Oscoda Beach Park opens directly onto Lake Huron near town, with a pier and broad sand. Watch how the waves approach and whether wind is coming from the lake. The nearby forecast describes the area; local flags and currents need attention at the shore.
notes.bird-creek-county-park: At Port Austin, Bird Creek reaches Lake Huron beside the beach and boardwalk. The creek mouth and the open lake are two different moving-water settings. Check wind and posted guidance before making a water decision, even when the town air feels calm.
notes.rogers-city-lakeside-park: Lakeside Park brings a sandy municipal beach into downtown Rogers City. Step toward Lake Huron and see whether the breeze feels different from nearby streets. Use the forecast for planning, and the current posted notices and visible conditions for decisions at the water.
